reader.title: Lynching of a cowboy at Deming
bases: The only account says the cowboy who shot a newcomer 'was lynched soon after' (A1), but gives no detail of who killed him or how, and nothing about race.

A1 says only that the cowboy 'was lynched soon after' killing a newcomer, which implies an extralegal killing in retribution, but it names no perpetrators or their number, gives no place more certain than 'Deming, I think', no date, and no race for anyone involved (A1).
One undated, unsourced anecdote in a Tennessee paper is the only report found (A1).

summary.text: The lynching of a cowboy at Deming is known from a single anecdote, headlined "Wild Shooting in Arizona," printed in The Home Journal of Winchester, Tennessee, on December 7, 1881.
According to the anecdote, an unnamed cowboy accidentally shot and killed a young newcomer in the street and "was lynched soon after."
The account gives no date, names, or race for anyone involved, and its writer was unsure even of the town.
The writer placed the episode "at Deming, I think," where "a bullying cowboy" had "about succeeded in taking the town."
A railroad employee and his companion, a young newcomer "just from the States," had been subjected to several displays of the cowboy's "lawlessness."
As the town grew excited, the newcomer remarked that someone would yet be killed and proposed to disarm the cowboy.
The cowboy galloped up and down the street firing his revolver, riding into saloons and stopping at them to drink.
Coming out of a saloon, he fired down the sidewalk and then, without looking, laid the pistol back over his shoulder and pulled the trigger.
The newcomer, stepping out of a nearby saloon at that moment, was struck in the forehead and fell dead.
The anecdote disposes of the cowboy's fate in one clause, saying only that he "was lynched soon after."
It does not say who killed him, how many took part, where or how he died, or whether he had first been arrested.
No report of an inquest, arrests, or any official response appears in the coverage, which consists of this one item.
The Home Journal ran the story on its front page as an unsigned, undated frontier sketch rather than as news, with no dateline or source.
Its writer called the cowboy a "crazy assassin" yet questioned the lynching, asking "but to what purpose?" and adding that nothing could atone for such a loss.
No other paper's version was found, and the item makes no mention of race.
